blocks.text: A plant manager must choose between a 50 000 GBP machine that wears out in five years and an 80 000 GBP machine that lasts eight. Comparing the purchase prices, or even the total cost of each over its own life, is misleading, because the machines do not serve the same number of years. Engineering economics gives three tools for fair comparison: payback, equivalent annual cost and a properly built cost estimate.

blocks.markdown: Project appraisal answers the question 'is it worth spending this money, and which option is better?' The tools differ in what they ignore. **Payback** is quick and intuitive; **equivalent annual cost** corrects for unequal lives and the time value of money; and a **cost estimate** is the input that all appraisal methods depend on. Money is in GBP throughout; the method is currency-independent.

blocks.title: Payback period
blocks.text: The time needed for the cumulative net cash inflow from an investment to equal the initial outlay. It is read from the cumulative cash flow, interpolating within the year in which the cumulative total crosses zero.

blocks.caption: I is the initial investment, C_N the cumulative net cash flow at the end of year N (the last year before recovery), and F_{N+1} the cash flow in the following year.

blocks.title: Payback with uneven cash flows
blocks.prompt: A 90 000 GBP investment returns net cash flows of 20 000, 30 000, 35 000 and 35 000 GBP in years 1 to 4. Find the payback period.

steps.text: Cumulative inflow: end of year 1 is 20 000; year 2 is 50 000; year 3 is 85 000; year 4 is 120 000.
Recovery occurs during year 4, since 85 000 is below 90 000 and 120 000 is above. So N = 3.

blocks.title: Limits of payback
blocks.text: Simple payback ignores cash flows after the payback date and ignores the time value of money. A project with a short payback can be worse overall than one with a longer payback and large later returns.

blocks.markdown: When two alternatives have **unequal lives**, comparing their total costs favours the shorter-lived one unfairly. The **equivalent annual cost (EAC)** spreads the initial cost over the life as a uniform annual amount, using an interest (discount) rate $i$, and adds the annual operating cost. The capital recovery factor converts a present sum into equal end-of-year payments over $n$ years.

blocks.caption: P is the initial cost, i the annual discount rate, n the life in years and A the annual operating cost; salvage value, if any, is subtracted from P first.

blocks.title: Choosing between machines of unequal life
blocks.prompt: Machine A costs 50 000 GBP, lasts 5 years and costs 8 000 GBP per year to run. Machine B costs 80 000 GBP, lasts 8 years and costs 6 000 GBP per year to run. Use a discount rate of 8% and no salvage value. Which has the lower EAC?

steps.text: Capital recovery factor for A (i = 0.08, n = 5):

blocks.answer: Machine B has the lower EAC, about 19 921 GBP per year against 20 523 GBP for A, despite the higher purchase price.

rows: Cash after payback; time value of money
Quick screening; risky or fast-changing markets
Benefits (only costs are compared); assumes replacement is identical
Choosing between alternatives of unequal life
Overall worth of a project with a defined horizon
blocks.caption: Appraisal methods compared.

blocks.markdown: Every appraisal depends on a credible **cost estimate**. A **bottom-up estimate** breaks the work into packages (materials, labour hours at a rate, subcontracts, testing), estimates each from quantities and rates, and sums them. A **contingency** is then added for uncertainty. Contingency is not padding: it is sized for each item according to how well it is understood, with larger percentages where the estimate is less certain.

blocks.title: Bottom-up estimate with contingency
blocks.prompt: A test rig is estimated as follows. Materials 14 500 GBP (uncertainty allowance 5%); labour 220 hours at 45 GBP per hour (15%); outsourced machining 6 200 GBP (10%); testing 3 000 GBP (20%). Find the base estimate, the contingency and the total.
blocks.answer: Total budget is 37 030 GBP: 33 600 GBP base plus 3 430 GBP contingency (about 10.2% of base).

blocks.title: State assumptions
blocks.text: Every figure in an appraisal depends on stated assumptions: discount rate, life, operating cost, whether replacement repeats the original, and the basis of the contingency. A result without them cannot be checked.

points: Payback is the time for cumulative net inflow to repay the outlay; it is simple but ignores later cash flows and the time value of money.
Equivalent annual cost spreads capital over the life using the capital recovery factor and adds running cost, allowing alternatives of unequal life to be compared fairly.
A bottom-up cost estimate sums itemised packages, then adds a contingency sized to the uncertainty of each item.

questions.stem: A new CNC fixture costs 46 000 GBP and is expected to save 11 500 GBP per year in scrap and set-up time, as a uniform annual net cash flow. What is the simple payback period in years?
questions.explanation: Payback is the investment divided by the uniform annual net saving: 46 000/11 500 = 4.0 years. The figure ignores any cash flow after year 4 and the time value of money.

questions.stem: A 60 000 GBP investment produces net cash flows of 10 000, 25 000, 30 000 and 30 000 GBP in years 1 to 4. What is the payback period?

distractorRationale.a: Cumulative inflow at the end of year 2 is only 35 000.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: cumulative is 35 000 after year 2 and 65 000 after year 3; payback is 2 + 25 000/30 000 = 2.83 years.
distractorRationale.c: 3.0 years would be the point at which 65 000 had been received, past the 60 000 needed.
distractorRationale.d: 3.5 years does not follow from the cumulative flows.

questions.explanation: Add the cash flows year by year: 10 000, then 35 000, then 65 000. Recovery of the 60 000 occurs in year 3, after 25 000 of the 30 000 in that year has been received, so payback is 2.83 years.

questions.stem: Which is the main weakness of simple payback as the sole basis for choosing between two projects?

options.text: It ignores cash flows after the payback date and the time value of money
It cannot be calculated if cash flows are uneven
It always favours the project with the longer life

questions.correctOptionText: It ignores cash flows after the payback date and the time value of money

distractorRationale.a: Simple payback does not use a discount rate; that is its simplicity.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a project with large later returns can be rejected, and delay of cash flows is not penalised.
distractorRationale.c: It can be calculated with uneven flows by interpolation.
distractorRationale.d: It tends to favour fast returns, not long life.

questions.explanation: Payback only tells you when the money is recovered. It says nothing about what happens afterwards, so it can rank a poorer project above a better one.

questions.stem: A hydraulic pump costs 12 000 GBP, lasts 4 years, has no salvage value and costs 2 500 GBP per year to operate. At a discount rate of 10% the capital recovery factor for 4 years is 0.3155. Calculate the equivalent annual cost in GBP per year.
questions.explanation: Capital charge: 12 000 x 0.3155 = 3 786 GBP per year. Adding the operating cost of 2 500 gives an EAC of about 6 286 GBP per year. The tolerance allows for rounding of the factor.

questions.stem: Why is equivalent annual cost used rather than total cost when choosing between a 6-year-life compressor and a 12-year-life compressor?

options.text: Because annual costs are always smaller
Because the machines provide service for different durations, so costs must be put on a common annual basis
Because operating costs can be ignored
Because discount rates do not apply to long-lived equipment

questions.correctOptionText: Because the machines provide service for different durations, so costs must be put on a common annual basis

distractorRationale.a: Size of the numbers is irrelevant.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: totals over different lives do not represent the same service period; EAC converts each to a yearly figure.
distractorRationale.c: Operating costs are included in EAC.
distractorRationale.d: Discounting applies to all lives; it is part of the EAC calculation.

questions.explanation: Total cost over life penalises the longer-lived machine because it buys more years of service. EAC converts capital to a yearly equivalent so that alternatives are compared on the same annual basis.

questions.stem: A bracket machining job is estimated bottom-up: stock 8 200 GBP (contingency allowance 5%), 150 hours of labour at 38 GBP per hour (20%), tooling 2 400 GBP (10%) and heat-treatment subcontract 1 900 GBP (15%). Calculate the total budget including contingency in GBP.
questions.explanation: Labour is 150 x 38 = 5 700 GBP, so the base is 8 200 + 5 700 + 2 400 + 1 900 = 18 200 GBP. Contingency items are 410, 1 140, 240 and 285 GBP, totalling 2 075 GBP. The total is 18 200 + 2 075 = 20 275 GBP.

questions.stem: In a bottom-up estimate, contingency should be a single flat percentage added without regard to how uncertain each item is.
questions.explanation: Contingency should reflect the uncertainty of each item: well-defined costs need little, poorly understood ones more. A single flat percentage may under-protect risky items and over-protect firm ones.

questions.stem: Project A needs 100 000 GBP and returns 60 000 GBP in year 1 and 40 000 GBP in year 2, with nothing after. Project B needs 100 000 GBP and returns 20 000, 30 000, 50 000 and 80 000 GBP in years 1 to 4. Calculate the payback period of each, state which has the shorter payback, and explain why that does not make it the better investment.
markingGuide: Project A payback: cumulative 60 000, then 100 000 at end of year 2, so payback 2.0 years
Project B payback: cumulative 20 000, 50 000, 100 000, so payback 3.0 years
B returns 180 000 GBP in total against 100 000 GBP for A, a net gain of 80 000 GBP against zero
Payback ignores cash flows after the payback date
Notes time value of money; recommends NPV or a similar method for ranking
questions.explanation: Both paybacks must be computed from cumulative flows. The key insight is that A merely returns its outlay while B continues to produce value after its payback date, which payback does not capture.

questions.stem: Compressor C costs 35 000 GBP, lasts 6 years and costs 4 200 GBP per year to run. Compressor D costs 50 000 GBP, lasts 12 years and costs 3 000 GBP per year to run. Neither has salvage value. At a discount rate of 7% the capital recovery factors are 0.2098 for 6 years and 0.1259 for 12 years. Calculate the EAC of each, state which you would choose, and state the main assumption of the method.
markingGuide: Chooses D as the lower EAC
Explains that EAC puts unequal lives on a common annual basis
Assumption: the shorter-lived option is replaced by an identical machine at the same cost, and the same discount rate applies
Notes that non-financial factors or uncertainty of long life may also matter
questions.explanation: The arithmetic should be shown. The marker also looks for the identical-replacement assumption of EAC and a recommendation consistent with the calculated figures.

questions.stem: You are asked to prepare a budget for building and testing a hydraulic test rig frame. Describe how you would build a bottom-up cost estimate and how you would set the contingency, giving examples of items with higher and lower uncertainty.
markingGuide: Breaks the work into packages such as materials, fabrication labour, bought-in components, testing and commissioning
Estimates quantities and unit rates for each (hours x rate, mass x price, quotations)
Sums the items to give a base estimate
Sets contingency per item according to uncertainty, such as lower for quoted components and higher for novel testing
Reviews the estimate and updates it as uncertainty reduces
questions.explanation: A good answer shows a transparent breakdown and a rationale for contingency tied to uncertainty rather than a flat allowance. Stating assumptions and exclusions is part of professional practice.
